questions.stem: For a responsive medical patient, what carries the greater diagnostic weight?

options.text: The physical examination
options.rationale: On a trauma patient the exam leads; on a medical patient it follows the history.

options.text: The history of the present illness and past history
options.rationale: Correct. The story usually tells you more than your hands do.

options.text: The mechanism of injury
options.rationale: Medical patients often have no mechanism at all.

options.text: The vital signs alone
options.rationale: Vitals matter but rarely name the problem on their own.

questions.stem: You arrive to find a medical patient unresponsive with no bystanders. What assessment path do you take?

options.text: Wait for family before doing anything
options.rationale: Assessment does not wait on a history that may never arrive.

options.text: Primary assessment, then a rapid head-to-toe and vital signs, gathering history from the scene
options.rationale: Correct. With no history available, the exam leads and the scene supplies what it can.

options.text: A focused exam of the chest only
options.rationale: A focused exam needs a history to focus it.

options.text: History only, from the patient's phone
options.rationale: The phone is not an assessment and the patient needs one now.

questions.stem: A patient with shortness of breath is talking to you in full sentences. What comes before the history?

options.rationale: Correct. The front of the call does not change because the patient is medical.

options.text: A full set of vital signs and nothing else
options.rationale: Vitals are part of the assessment but do not replace the primary.

options.text: Transport decision
options.rationale: A transport decision is made from an assessment, not before one.

options.text: Every 30 minutes

questions.stem: How should the chief complaint be documented?

options.text: As your field impression
options.rationale: The impression is yours; the complaint is the patient's.

options.text: In the patient's own words, quoted
options.rationale: Correct. The quote is data; a diagnosis written in its place is a guess.

options.text: As the dispatch code
options.rationale: Dispatch information is often wrong and is not the patient's complaint.

options.text: As the most likely diagnosis

questions.stem: An 82-year-old says only that she feels weak and not right. How should this be regarded?

options.text: As a social call requiring no assessment
options.rationale: Every patient gets an assessment.

options.text: As anxiety until proven otherwise

options.rationale: Hemorrhagic strokes are the minority.

options.text: Ischemic
options.rationale: Correct. A blocked vessel is by far the more common mechanism.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack
options.rationale: A TIA resolves completely and is not a completed stroke.

options.text: They occur at equal rates

questions.stem: Why do blood sugar problems present as neurological problems?

options.text: Because glucose is only used by the brain
options.rationale: Every cell uses glucose; the brain is simply most vulnerable.

options.text: Because the brain cannot store fuel and cannot quickly switch to another
options.rationale: Correct. It feels a supply problem before anywhere else does.

options.text: Because insulin acts directly on nerve tissue
options.rationale: That is not the mechanism described.

options.text: Because diabetes damages nerves over time
options.rationale: True of chronic disease, but not why acute dysglycaemia alters mental status.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient has had influenza for three days. Which direction would you expect the glucose to move?

options.text: Down, because illness reduces appetite
options.rationale: Reduced intake pulls one way, but illness raises demand more.

options.text: Up, because illness and infection raise blood glucose
options.rationale: Correct. Being unwell commonly drives glucose higher, not lower.

options.text: It will be unchanged
options.rationale: Intercurrent illness rarely leaves glucose unchanged.

options.text: It cannot be predicted at all, so no meter is needed
options.rationale: A meter is always used, but illness does have an expected direction.

questions.stem: A hypoglycemic patient is unresponsive. What is the correct action regarding oral glucose?

options.text: Withhold it; manage the airway, transport, and seek advanced-level intervention

options.rationale: Liquid is worse, not better, in an unprotected airway.

questions.stem: Why is hypoglycemia considered more time-critical than hyperglycemia?

options.text: Because it is more common
options.rationale: Frequency is not the reason.

options.text: Because the brain is being deprived of fuel immediately
options.rationale: Correct. A high sugar builds over days; a low one starves the brain now.

options.text: Because it always causes a seizure
options.rationale: It can, but that is not the reason for urgency.

options.text: Because it cannot be treated in the field
options.rationale: It often can be, which is part of why finding it matters.
